> A pocket-sized synth keyboard with a button for every note, an OLED that shows the waveform live, and a mode switch for different instrument sounds. Press several keys at once to play chords and make your own music. It’s built on a custom KiCad PCB with the keys laid out like a tiny piano.

## Design

### 2026-10-25 – MiniMelody: 16 hours from "what should I build?" to a finished PCB

**15h**

MiniMelody: 16 hours from "what should I build?" to a finished PCB

This week started with a blank form and the words "make some noise." Four days and 16 hours later, I have a full schematic, a routed PCB, and a 3D render of a pocket synth that I designed myself. I worked about 4 hours a day, and I planned the whole thing with Claude (an AI assistant) as a thinking partner, checking and deciding each step myself. Here's how it went, hour by hour.

 Day 1: Dreaming it up

**Hour 1.** I started with the Music Week brief and a pile of ideas: a light theremin, a drone box, a motion synth. None of them felt like mine until I imagined a tiny piano I could carry, with a button for every note, a screen, and a proper speaker. The best part was being able to press several buttons at once to play chords.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/83wHhG3lcEmAv3SucuBTvqFHVoYz3xIc/d493d2447f6382fc9102b94c281f70d5444c942d7ef8ba45a82629d9219db675.png)

**Hour 2.** Chords turned out to be the hard part, because a basic Arduino can only play one note at a time. So I chose a Raspberry Pi Pico, which is fast enough to mix several notes, plus a MAX98357A amplifier for clean sound and an OLED to show what's playing. I also cut the keyboard from 12 keys to 8 to keep the board small.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/83wHhG3lcEmAv3SucuBTvqFHVoYz3xIc/eaec7ef312d5624ddcb2979e104302b0d621021b879e83ded1caf9d06abaac12.png)

**Hour 3.** I sketched where everything should go: keys in a row along the bottom, the screen at the top-left, and the speaker at the top-right, with the controls in between.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/83wHhG3lcEmAv3SucuBTvqFHVoYz3xIc/d3ed587c0954f423424fbea510de707d3dd519c361ad7594e2621cf95d912791.png)

**Hour 4.** I made two big decisions. First, a PCB instead of a breadboard, because 11 buttons plus audio plus a screen would be a nest of loose wires. Second, every button goes straight to its own Pico pin using the Pico's built-in pull-up resistors, so I needed no diodes and no extra resistors.

![Screenshot from 2026-10-24 11-52-34](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/83wHhG3lcEmAv3SucuBTvqFHVoYz3xIc/2ab4e3a5a926a4674d34207f860279b0e6d5b950ef4dbfa5af65bdb1f0188d77.png)

## Day 2: Gathering parts and starting the schematic

**Hour 5.** I hunted for the symbol, footprint, and 3D model of every part. I used KiCad's built-in libraries first and downloaded the rest.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/83wHhG3lcEmAv3SucuBTvqFHVoYz3xIc/5cb6c05819ddf0d6cb59a5c8e08f93b46781e0109f989841ad712a362c56abd3.png)

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/83wHhG3lcEmAv3SucuBTvqFHVoYz3xIc/306bb8aeabb7e9699128d78e9062a9b6f38c7628ecf0a42f4a4eea9952e61ea7.png)

**Hour 6.** The speaker isn't in KiCad's libraries, so I made it a simple 2-pin connector and drew my own footprint. Lesson learned: always check a footprint against the datasheet.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/83wHhG3lcEmAv3SucuBTvqFHVoYz3xIc/a620dbeb6907de7222b3e6ef6c76758b2b10589abc4f20c878e73e3ead10872a.png)

**Hour 7.** I drew the buttons and the Pico connections, using net labels instead of long messy wires.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/83wHhG3lcEmAv3SucuBTvqFHVoYz3xIc/fe630bfc655d5a474998d27f0bb48f42d6c9da4a45bf71a231007fc1154b08fd.png)

**Hour 8.** I added the amplifier, display, and power. My first draft had real mistakes, like the amplifier on the wrong supply voltage.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/83wHhG3lcEmAv3SucuBTvqFHVoYz3xIc/35df814948626e20153ebee4399d10069846bfbb12ab4080c87d00b37f9e9fad.png)

## Day 3: Debugging

**Hour 9.** I fixed the power and ground wiring, moved the amplifier to 5 V, kept the OLED on 3.3 V, and rewired the rotary encoder correctly. I also deleted a USB-C connector I didn't need, because the Pico already has its own USB port.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/83wHhG3lcEmAv3SucuBTvqFHVoYz3xIc/80ce3d1f83278578d805bba9d9a97a13e6b63478041ec9cd8f6a0435bdaac53f.png)

**Hour 10.** I ran KiCad's Electrical Rules Checker and worked through every error. Each one taught me something: PWR_FLAG symbols, why two supply labels can end up as two separate nets, and why every part needs a reference name.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/83wHhG3lcEmAv3SucuBTvqFHVoYz3xIc/e77a0ecdda4c8d5195b399119172feaf8de357654bb9410e59cb0c8ed0c8acaa.png)

**Hour 11.** I assigned a footprint to every part and fixed the ones that didn't match the real components.
📸 *Screenshot: the footprint assignment window*

**Hour 12.** I moved the design into the PCB editor and arranged the parts. Seeing the tangle of thin ratsnest lines was exciting and a little scary.

![Screenshot from 2026-10-23 18-20-23](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/83wHhG3lcEmAv3SucuBTvqFHVoYz3xIc/e3d3290dd0ed502e43c88d383d4e084be39382ccc99d7e6f16eb647fe1c590e0.png)

![Screenshot from 2026-10-22 21-26-28](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/83wHhG3lcEmAv3SucuBTvqFHVoYz3xIc/9c0f5a0c2e0f70bfcf52f3c5facc33071bbb419a3d46852fa6ec8598d79489a4.png)

## Day 4: Routing and checking

**Hour 13.** I set the trace widths (thicker for power, thinner for signals) and added the mounting holes.

![Screenshot from 2026-10-23 18-20-23](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/83wHhG3lcEmAv3SucuBTvqFHVoYz3xIc/e3d3290dd0ed502e43c88d383d4e084be39382ccc99d7e6f16eb647fe1c590e0.png)

**Hour 14.** I connected all the parts with traces. A few things went wrong, but I fixed them quickly because of everything the earlier days had taught me.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/83wHhG3lcEmAv3SucuBTvqFHVoYz3xIc/e1d92f03e15e1f862960ded6fe3179affe775d82afbf5627338720780b0fb313.png)

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/83wHhG3lcEmAv3SucuBTvqFHVoYz3xIc/aadd2a35061308cbe7e2c58517794c24cdf712f7054192715803bea5a3109b43.png)

**Hour 15.** I added the copper ground fill and cleaned up the messy areas.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/83wHhG3lcEmAv3SucuBTvqFHVoYz3xIc/e1d92f03e15e1f862960ded6fe3179affe775d82afbf5627338720780b0fb313.png)

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/83wHhG3lcEmAv3SucuBTvqFHVoYz3xIc/28b1350c50b62c622f79b0784f40c26f65de00bd840b70b4c7cec705d5d23d71.png)

**Hour 16.** I opened the 3D viewer to check that everything lines up. It looked great, and it also showed me that the board outline needs fixing. I also started the README and the firmware plan for the Pico.

![Screenshot from 2026-10-23 18-20-23](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/83wHhG3lcEmAv3SucuBTvqFHVoYz3xIc/e3d3290dd0ed502e43c88d383d4e084be39382ccc99d7e6f16eb647fe1c590e0.png)

## The real-life part

Where I live, the power supply isn't stable, and it cut out several times while I was working. That slowed me down and made me save constantly, but I still finished the schematic and the PCB layout.

## What I learned

- Planning first saves a lot of time later.
- The Electrical Rules Checker is annoying but very useful.
- Always check footprints against the datasheet.

 Next

Fix the board outline and the last unrouted connection, run the Design Rules Check, order the board, and write the firmware, starting with one key making one sound.
